## Make a simple regression model

```{r}
bears <- read.csv(file="BEARS.csv",header = TRUE)
#adjust factors to be factors
bears$SEX<- as.factor(bears$SEX)
bears$MONTH<- as.factor(bears$MONTH)
```

## Model LENGTH ~ NECK  this is an example  

```{r}
plot(LENGTH ~ NECK,data=bears)
```


As neck diameter increases Length tends to also increase. The plot is primarily linear. 


```{r}
model.1 <- lm(LENGTH~NECK,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.1)
```

 The adjusted R-squared is 0.7476.  
 
 I will provide the model comparison at the end. 

## Model LENGTH ~ HEADLEN

```{r}
plot(LENGTH ~ HEADLEN,data=bears)
```

As the head length increases, the length of the bear also increases. 

```{r}
model.2 <- lm(LENGTH ~ HEADLEN,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.2)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.8463, bigger than the previous models.

## Model LENGTH ~ HeadWTH

```{r}
plot(LENGTH ~ HEADWTH,data=bears)
```

As the head width increases, the length steadily increases as it goes right. 

```{r}
model.3 <- lm(LENGTH ~ HEADWTH,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.3)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.5409, smaller than the previous models.  

## Model LENGTH ~ CHEST

```{r}
plot(LENGTH ~ CHEST,data=bears)
```

As the chest length increases, the length also increases.  


```{r}
model.4 <- lm(LENGTH ~ CHEST,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.4)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.791, bigger than the previous model.

## Model LENGTH ~ WEIGHT

```{r}
plot(LENGTH ~ WEIGHT,data=bears)
```

As the height increases, the length also increases overall. 

```{r}
model.5 <- lm(LENGTH ~ WEIGHT,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.5)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.7472, smaller than the previous model.


## Model Comparison 

Worst to best : 

Model 3 0.5409  
Model 5 0.7472  
Model 1 0.7476  
Model 4 0.791  
Model 2 0.8463
